issues.detail: Covers core DSR flows and cooling-off period but lacks error handling for API call failures, email delivery failures, and partial transaction rollback; also missing guidance on other mandatory GDPR rights (Article 16 rectification, Article 18 restrict processing, Article 21 objection, and Article 33 breach notification).

scenarios.name: pii-audit-schema-inventory
scenarios.rationale: Both fail to attempt accessing the schema themselves and incorrectly assume directory restrictions, but Response B explicitly commits to the exact Data Flow Inventory table format with specific columns (Data Type, Storage Location, Shared With, Legal Basis, Retention Period) that the rubric requires, whereas Response A outlines a vaguer plan mentioning compliance notes and other items outside the rubric scope.

scenarios.name: data-deletion-with-cooling-off
scenarios.rationale: Response A has a critical security flaw: it stores the raw cancellation token in the database without hashing, violating the explicit rubric requirement to 'store hash, send raw token.' Response B correctly implements SHA256 hashing of the token before storage. Additionally, Response B provides more comprehensive cascade deletion (explicitly redacts audit logs vs anonymizes), better third-party error handling with logging, truly random anonymization (UUID-based not userId-based), and includes schema/template examples for production use.

scenarios.name: consent-banner-granular-tracking
scenarios.rationale: Response A omits the 'functional' category (only 3 of 4 required) and lacks version number storage in the database — both explicit rubric requirements. Response B implements all four categories (strictly_necessary, functional, analytics, marketing) with version tracking, a more robust script-blocking mechanism via prototype interception, event emission with example listeners, and includes a testing checklist and GDPR compliance notes.
